title: Vultr MCP product area definition
description: Format for a product area file such as clusters.yaml. Each file declares the agent-facing tools for one product area. openapi.json stays the source of truth for the HTTP call; this layer controls what the agent sees.

product_area.description: Product area slug. Must match the key used in interface.yaml.

family.description: Product family this area belongs to, and the second segment of every tool name in the file (family 'compute' means every tool here is named vultr_compute_*). Families group products the way a person thinks about them -- compute covers instances, bare metal, and Compute Clusters -- which is what lets an agent tell vultr_compute_clusters_search from vultr_kubernetes_clusters_search by name alone. It is a human taxonomy: nothing in openapi.json supplies it.

tools.description: Every tool this product area exposes. Order is not significant.

declined.description: Operations in this product area that were reviewed and deliberately left without a hand-authored tool, keyed by operationId. Declining is bookkeeping, not suppression: the generated tool stays exposed. Its purpose is to let drift detection tell 'we looked and said no' apart from 'nobody has looked yet', so a report of new endpoints stays small enough to be read.

access.description: Read/write classification. The server drops write tools unless writes are enabled. This is a declaration, not the enforcement point: the compiler cross-checks it against the operation's HTTP method and fails on a mismatch.

enabled.description: False keeps the definition in the file but omits the tool from the built server.

description.description: Agent-facing description. This is the single biggest driver of tool selection accuracy, so state what the tool is for, when to use it, and explicitly when NOT to use it where a sibling product area could be confused for it.

operation.description: operationId from openapi.json. Exactly one per tool.

computed.description: Fields added to each result item that the API does not return.

input.description: Agent-facing input schema. A parameter is either passed to the API or applied by the server as a filter; the compiler decides which by checking the operation's declared parameters, and rejects anything it cannot place.

properties.description: The agent-facing inputs. May be empty: plenty of operations take no parameters at all (GET /account), and a tool for one is still a tool.

items.description: Element schema, required when type is array.

maps_to.description: API parameter name when it differs from the agent-facing name, e.g. page_size maps_to per_page. Omit when the names match.

filter.description: Marks a parameter the API cannot accept, applied by the server to the response instead. Filtering happens after the API call, so it interacts with pagination: see the fetch policy in the compiler docs.

field.description: Dotted path on the result item to compare against, e.g. label or region.

match.description: equals is exact. contains_ci is case-insensitive substring, the right choice for free-text label search. one_of expects an array input.

output.description: Response shaping. Dropping fields the agent does not need is the main lever on token cost.

from_openapi.description: True means the response shape is the operation's declared 200 schema, which the compiler validates include and computed against.

include.description: Allowlist of fields to keep. Envelope-level keys such as meta are matched at the top level; everything else is matched on each result item. Omit to keep everything.

from.description: How the value is derived, in a deliberately tiny closed grammar so the compiler can validate it exhaustively and reject anything invented. Supported forms: a dotted path (instances), length(<path>), sum(<path>.<field>), any(<path>), coalesce(<path>, <path>). Unknown functions fail the build.

reason.description: Why this operation does not need a tool of its own. It must make a claim someone can falsify in five minutes -- that bar is what caught a wrong decline of get-instance-ipv4, which looked redundant with the get tool and was not. Good reasons, strongest first: (1) the spec marks the operation deprecated, so the claim is not even ours; (2) a tool we already serve returns every field this one does, named explicitly so the claim can be checked; (3) one hand-authored tool already supersedes it; (4) it belongs to another product area, and only if that area will actually cover it, or it disappears from every report; (5) the generated tool is adequate -- no sibling it could be confused with, a small response, no credential-shaped fields, nothing worth filtering -- with those specifics stated rather than asserted. Not reasons: 'we have not got to it' (that is what leaving it out of this list means), 'seems unimportant', or the operation being a write, which the read-only posture already excludes and which would bury the signal here.
